chunks.text: Primary sedimentation is to remove the suspended solids (SS) by controlling the water flow velocity. It is required the settling time of SS shorter than the water travelling time in the tank. The SS with low density (1.1 g/mL and 1.5 g/mL) or small size but high density (1.5 g/mL) is the target pollutants to be removed in primary clarification. Most abundant MPs in the wastewater is PET followed by PE and PP (Fig. 2b ). The density of PET is between 0.96 and 1.45 g/mL. It is predicted that the primary sedimentation would catch the MPs consist of PET. However, PE and PP are difficult to be removed as they have density lower than water. Hence, wastewater containing large amount of moderate-density MPs would have high MPs removal during primary treatment.

chunks.text: A pilot-scale system, consisting of a grit tank and microscreen for primary treatment followed by a SAF-MBR 2.0 for secondary treatment, was installed at the Codiga Resource Recovery Center (Stanford, CA), as illustrated in. The pilot-scale system treated municipal wastewater pumped from the Serra Street sewer on the Stanford campus for more than three years. Sewage was de-gritted in a grit tank then subject to primary treatment by screening through a 0.3 mm pore size microscreen (MS-28, Hydro International). The pilot-scale SAF-MBR 2.0 consisted of: (1) two AFBRs operated in parallel, hereafter referred to as AFBR 1 and AFBR 2, containing fluidized GAC biocarrier, and (2) a gas-sparged membrane tank equipped with ultrafiltration membranes. Recirculation of bulk fluid (twice the influent flow rate) between the three reactors enabled complete mixing and control of solids accumulation within the gas-sparged membrane tank.

chunks.text: Screens and grit removal are widely employed in WWTPs as they enhance the operation and maintenance of subsequent treatment units. Recent innovations in pretreatment technologies have brought the heavy cost of grit in WWTPs operations lower which has been considered an unavoidable burden. For example, based on advanced Grit Management™, Headcell® grit separation system was developed to achieve optimum grit removal for more than 30 years in the UK and USA. Headcell® is capable of achieving 95% removal of all grit 75 μm and larger. Because of its no-moving part design involving a hydraulically driven system, it delivers grit removal over a wide range of flows in a much smaller energy footprint than the conventional removal systems (Barter and Sherony, 2011) . Table 5 lists several such advanced technologies currently being considered for pilot, demonstration, and full-scale operations in the North America.

chunks.text: Nitrification is an essential process for nitrogen removal from wastewater, comprising two steps, i.e., the oxidation of ammonium (NH 4 + ) to nitrite (NO 2 − ), and then to nitrate (NO 3 − ). In a wastewater treatment system, nitrification usually occurs at a neutral pH (∼7) with NO 3 − as the final product when the oxygen supply is unlimited. Nitrification at an acidic pH was recently suggested as a novel process for wastewater treatment. At a slightly acidic pH range (4.5−5.5), it was found that the end product of nitrification tends to be NO 2 − instead of NO 3 − , even with high dissolved oxygen (DO > 4 mg O 2 / L). 1,2 However, acidic nitrification without considerable NO 2 − accumulation has also been widely reported in literature. 3−5 Tarre et al. 4 observed NO 3 − accumulation in suspended-and attached-biomass reactors at pH of ∼4, in which nitriteoxidizing bacteria (NOB) Nitrobacter existed in large aggregates.

chunks.text: However, these processes are costly, require high energy consumption and generally produce secondary waste which cannot remove the pollutants completely and then puts more pressure on the environment (Ghafari et al., 2008; Kapoor and Viraraghavan, 1997) . In contrast, biological treatment is generally regarded as a better choice for nitrate removal from wastewater due to its advantages of complete contaminants removal, economical and energy-saving. Currently, the complete denitrification process is widely applied for nitrate-containing wastewater treatment (Gu et al., 2015; Song et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2020) . However, the traditional complete denitrification process (Eqs. ( 1 ) and ( 2 )) still presents some shortcomings, including high operational costs due to external organic carbon source requirements (Gu et al., 2015; Song et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2020) , large amounts of sludge yields and inevitable greenhouse gas emission, etc. (Du et al., 2016b) . Partial denitrification (PD) refers to the process of controlling NO 3 − -N reduced to NO 2 − -N without further reducing to nitrogen gas (N 2 ).

chunks.text: Belkacem et al. [29] reported the use of reverse osmosis for the treatment of groundwater with 95 % removal of TDS and 97 % reduction in conductivity. Srinivasan et al. [30] used spiral bound reverse osmosis membranes for recovery of phenolic compounds. The combination of NF and RO membrane have also been demonstrated which resulted in significant improvement in the removal of COD and TDS with decrease in conductivity. Nataraj et al. [31] used membrane-based nanofiltration and reverse osmosis process combination for treatment of distillery wastewater which resulted in 99.8 % TDS reduction, 99.9 % COD reduction and 99.99 % potassium removal. The use of the membrane process is associated with serval drawbacks like fouling, flux decline, secondary waste generation and requirement of repetitive chemical cleaning especially for the streams having higher COD concentrations [32] . The membrane bioreactor (MBR) is one of the important process for treatment of sewage water. However, membrane fouling has been reported as one of the major drawback of MBR due to activated sludge liquor, biological flocs and soluble colloidal compounds.

chunks.text: A ceramic ultrafiltration tubular module (UF50n, Atech) was tested for the elimination of suspended solids. The module contains an active layer of TiO 2 with an average pore diameter of 50 nm. The tube has an inner diameter of 6 mm and a length of 500 mm. The filtration experiments were conducted in a cross flow plant which allows the recirculation of permeate and retentate as well as a continuous removal of permeate. The experiments were done at a constant temperature of 30 C, a transmembrane pressure difference of 2.1 bar, a cross flow velocity along the membrane of 4 m/s and a backwash interval of 16 min with 10 s backwash duration. An amount of 63 L LOPROX effluent was recycled in the plant, so that the concentrations were kept constant for 25 h. After this the permeate was removed and therefore the concentration of suspended solids increased up to a permeate recovery (¼V P /V Fa ) of 83%.

Approximately 70% of the product water recharges groundwater using spreading ponds (basins) in Anaheim, California, which is blended with stormwater and imported/purchased water (OCWD, 2019a) . When the systems' capacity was 265,000 m 3 /day, water was produced at a unit cost of $0.56/m 3 (capital and O&M) and conveyance costs amounted to an additional $0.10/m 3 (Raucher & Tchobanoglous, 2014) .

chunks.text: A mass of 300 kg of screenings was sampled from the municipal wastewater treatment plant of Bourg-en-Bresse (Region Rhône-   Alpes, France). The waste was made of a mix of screenings from 15-mm and 3-mm screens and was compacted in the plant. The sample was taken to the laboratory where it was homogenized and divided into 20 sub-samples of 8 kg. The procedure allowed to guarantee a good reproducibility of the sub-samples composition, which was verified analytically. The samples were stored at À18 °C. A digestate sampled from a municipal solid waste (MSW) digester was used as an inoculum, in order to have active microflora and to make easier the start-up of anaerobic process.
